col.background: Colossians was written by Paul while in prison, addressed to the church at Colossae — a church Paul had not personally founded, but which was planted through the preaching of Epaphras. At the time, the church was being influenced by a false teaching that mixed in angel worship, legalistic regulations, and human philosophy, diminishing Christ's rightful place. The letter falls into two parts: the doctrinal section (chapters 1–2) emphasizes that Christ is the full expression of God himself, head over all creation and head of the church, and that believers are already made complete in him; the practical section (chapters 3–4) exhorts believers to put off the old self and put on the new, addressing household relationships between husbands and wives, parents and children, and masters and servants, before closing with greetings and instructions to exchange letters with the church at Laodicea.
col.keyPoints: The core message is the supreme sufficiency of Christ: he is the full expression of God and head over all things; believers are already complete in him, and are called to reject false, man-made regulations and live out a new life united with him.

rom.background: Romans is a letter written by the apostle Paul to the church in Rome, composed near the end of his third missionary journey, before he carried the collection to Jerusalem. It is the most systematic theological treatise among the New Testament epistles. The letter divides into two main parts: doctrine (chapters 1–11) and life (chapters 12–16). The doctrinal section first argues that all humanity — Jew and Gentile alike — stands guilty of sin, and that no one can be justified by keeping the law, but only by faith; it goes on to address sanctification, peace with God, the indwelling Holy Spirit, and God's election of and plan of salvation for Israel. The practical section then urges believers to offer themselves as living sacrifices, to love one another, to submit to governing authorities, and to bear with those weak in faith.
rom.keyPoints: The central truth is justification by faith: all have sinned, yet are freely justified through faith by the redemption that is in Christ Jesus; believers are called to live out a life of holiness in response.

2sa.background: 2 Samuel continues 1 Samuel, recounting the history of David's reign after Saul's death — first as king over Judah, then anointed king over all Israel — spanning roughly forty years on the throne. The first part (chapters 1-10) tells of his rise: he captures Jerusalem as his capital, and the LORD makes an everlasting covenant of kingship with him. The second part (chapters 11-20) turns to his fall: his sin with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah bring a chain of family tragedy - Amnon's rape of Tamar, Absalom's rebellion, and David's forced flight from Jerusalem. A closing appendix (chapters 21-24) records a famine, a roster of David's mighty men, and the plague brought on by his census.
2sa.keyPoints: The heart of the book is the LORD's everlasting covenant with David, the foundation of the messianic promise; it also shows sin's heavy cost, and God's faithful, disciplining rule even amid human weakness.
